newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to address Russians, face Duma criticism.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to address Russians, face Duma criticism.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin delivers on Friday his first radio address to the nation since he fell ill with pneumonia and his parliamentary foes are set to debate a non-binding resolution demanding that he quit.
But Yeltsin's representative in the State Duma lower house of parliament said on Thursday that the resolution would have "no consequences except political scandal".

Yeltsin, 66, was laid low with pneumonia five weeks ago, but he has slowly resumed a schedule of meetings with ministers, both at the suburban residence where he is convalescing and in his Kremlin office.

There have been brief television appearances, most of them without sound, and, apart a 45-second televised statement last week, he has not explained how he plans to deal with the many problems facing Russia.
Kremlin press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Interfax news agency that Yeltsin's radio address, to be broadcast at 11 a.m. (0800 GMT), would focus on pensions,
He said Yeltsin was angry at suggestions by the head of the Russian Pension Fund, Vassily Barchuk, that working pensioners could forfeit their right to a pension.
It was not known if Yeltsin would also address the situation in Tajikistan, where rebels have seized a group of Western and Russian hostages.
Reporters among the hostages said the rebels had killed a U.N. military observer, but the report could not be confirmed.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin early on Friday warned Russia will take all necessary means to save the lives of the hostages but said he hoped they would be released by Friday morning.

Speaking to reporters after a late-night government meeting on Thursday, Chernomyrdin said Moscow, which has a sizeable military presence in Tajikistan, had alerted its security officials about the situation after a United Nations military observer was reported killed, Itar-Tass news agency said.
Tass said Chernomyrdin, who is Russia's highest-profile political figure while Yeltsin recovers, had spoken to Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin would also address Moscow's relations with breakaway Chechnya and the possibility of constitutional reform.
Chechnya inaugurated a new president on Thursday.
Yeltsin's last radio address was in late December, a few days after he returned to the Kremlin following his quintuple heart surgery in November.

The president's growing activity has not silenced his critics in parliament who plan again to debate a non-binding resolution to force him from power on health grounds. Previous efforts to pass the resolution have failed.
Legal experts say the parliament cannot remove the president from office on health grounds.
